emails.subject: Deadlines vs. schedules: which one is better for goal achievement?

paragraphs.en: Hey 張振輝,
paragraphs.zh: 嗨 張振輝,

paragraphs.en: I'm torn between the two.
paragraphs.zh: 我在這兩者之間猶豫不決。

paragraphs.en: On the one hand, I'm a big believer in setting deadlines when it comes to setting goals.
paragraphs.zh: 一方面,在設定目標時,我非常相信「設定截止日期」的重要性。

paragraphs.en: I think it's important to see our destination accompanied by a target date. It helps us to prioritize tasks. It also helps us to allocate our limited attentional resources (time, focus, etc.).
paragraphs.zh: 我認為,看見目的地並搭配一個目標日期是很重要的。這有助於我們排定任務的優先順序,也有助於我們分配有限的注意力資源(時間、專注力等)。

paragraphs.en: At the same time, I'm also a huge advocate of putting goal-oriented tasks on a schedule.
paragraphs.zh: 但與此同時,我也十分提倡把以目標為導向的任務排進「行事曆」中。

paragraphs.en: That way, we don't have to rely on willpower to do them. We simply note the time of day, check our schedule to see what we should be doing, and get to it.
paragraphs.zh: 這樣一來,我們就不必依賴意志力去完成它們。我們只需留意當下的時間,查看行事曆上該做什麼,然後去做就好。

paragraphs.en: Can these two tactics coexist?
paragraphs.zh: 這兩種做法能夠並存嗎?

paragraphs.en: There's a lot of talk about deadlines versus schedules, and which option leads to greater success.
paragraphs.zh: 關於截止日期與行事曆孰優孰劣,一直有很多討論。

paragraphs.en: Both tactics have their supporters and detractors. And some of these folks are pretty vehement about their opinions.
paragraphs.zh: 這兩種做法都各有支持者與反對者。有些人對自己的看法還相當堅持。

paragraphs.en: Here's the thing...
paragraphs.zh: 事情是這樣的……

paragraphs.en: You don't need to choose. In my opinion, you should set deadlines AND schedules whenever you set goals.
paragraphs.zh: 你不需要二選一。依我之見,設定目標時,你應該同時設定截止日期「與」行事曆。

paragraphs.en: Here's a personal example to show you how they work together:
paragraphs.zh: 這裡有一個親身經歷的例子,讓你看看它們是如何協同運作的:

paragraphs.en: I recently finishing writing my latest book (more details coming in a few weeks). Before I wrote the first word, I opened up a monthly calendar in Google Calendar. Then, I chose a target date by which I wanted to complete the first draft.
paragraphs.zh: 我最近剛寫完我的新書(幾週後會有更多細節)。在寫下第一個字之前,我先在 Google 日曆中打開一個月曆。然後,我選定了一個希望完成初稿的目標日期。

paragraphs.en: So far, so good.
paragraphs.zh: 到目前為止都還不錯。

paragraphs.en: Next, I created an action plan. I worked backward from the target date, and I determined how much I'd need to write each day to achieve my goal.
paragraphs.zh: 接著,我制定了一個行動計畫。我從目標日期往回推算,確定每天需要寫多少字才能達成目標。

paragraphs.en: Finally, I scheduled writing time on my daily calendar. I decided to write from 5:30 a.m. to 7:30 a.m.
paragraphs.zh: 最後,我把寫作時間排進了每日行事曆。我決定從早上 5:30 寫到 7:30。

paragraphs.en: Every day. Monday through Sunday.
paragraphs.zh: 每天都是,週一到週日。

paragraphs.en: Can you guess what happened?
paragraphs.zh: 你猜發生了什麼事?

paragraphs.en: I finished the first draft by the target date. But here's the best part...
paragraphs.zh: 我在目標日期前完成了初稿。但最棒的部分是……

paragraphs.en: It wasn't difficult at all. I didn't need to rely on willpower to write. Nor did I need to "get motivated" or inspired or whisper affirmations to myself.
paragraphs.zh: 這一點都不困難。我不需要依賴意志力去寫作,也不需要「找動力」、尋求靈感,或對自己喃喃唸著肯定語句。

paragraphs.en: I simply looked at the clock each morning, saw that it was 5:30 a.m., and started writing.
paragraphs.zh: 我只是每天早上看看時鐘,發現是 5:30,然後就開始寫作。

paragraphs.en: The rest took care of itself.
paragraphs.zh: 剩下的事情自然就水到渠成了。

paragraphs.en: That's how deadlines and schedules can work together to help you to achieve your goals.
paragraphs.zh: 這就是截止日期與行事曆如何協同運作,幫助你達成目標。

paragraphs.en: Try the following...
paragraphs.zh: 試試看以下做法……

paragraphs.en: Choose one of your goals. It doesn't matter whether it's to learn a new language, run a marathon, or write a novel. Any goal will do.
paragraphs.zh: 選擇你的其中一個目標。無論是學一門新語言、跑一場馬拉松,還是寫一本小說,任何目標都可以。

paragraphs.en: Open up Google Calendar and select a target date. Make sure it's practical given your available time.
paragraphs.zh: 打開 Google 日曆,選定一個目標日期。務必確保它在你可運用的時間內是切實可行的。

paragraphs.en: Next, create an action plan to hit that date.
paragraphs.zh: 接著,制定一個能達成該日期的行動計畫。

paragraphs.en: For example, let's say you want to learn a new language. Commit to listening for 30 minutes each day to podcasts that offer lessons in that language.
paragraphs.zh: 舉例來說,假設你想學一門新語言,就承諾每天花 30 分鐘聽提供該語言課程的 Podcast。

paragraphs.en: Finally, put that activity on your daily schedule. Try to schedule it at the same time each day.
paragraphs.zh: 最後,把這項活動排進你的每日行事曆。盡量每天在同一個時間安排它。

paragraphs.en: After a couple weeks, you'll find yourself doing it as part of your daily routine. Easy peasy.
paragraphs.zh: 幾週之後,你會發現這已經成為你日常routine的一部分了。輕輕鬆鬆。

paragraphs.en: That's it for now.
paragraphs.zh: 今天就談到這裡。

paragraphs.en: Stay well and talk soon,
paragraphs.zh: 保重,咱們再聊,

paragraphs.en: Damon
paragraphs.zh: Damon

paragraphs.en: P.S. If you're not sure how to set goals you'll actually achieve, check out my book The P.R.I.M.E.R. Goal Setting Method. It'll take you, step-by-step guide, through the entire process.
paragraphs.zh: P.S. 如果你不確定該如何設定真正能達成的目標,可以看看我的書《The P.R.I.M.E.R. Goal Setting Method》。它會用逐步引導的方式,帶你走過整個流程。

emails.subject: 3 ways to bounce back after breaking your habit streak

paragraphs.en: Hey 張振輝,
paragraphs.zh: 嗨 張振輝,

paragraphs.en: Forming new habits is tough.
paragraphs.zh: 養成新習慣是件苦差事。

paragraphs.en: Whenever we adopt a new habit, we must train ourselves to do something that runs counter to our current routines. These routines can be so deeply ingrained that they seem impossible to break.
paragraphs.zh: 每當我們想採納一個新習慣,就必須訓練自己做一些與目前routine背道而馳的事。而這些routine往往根深蒂固,幾乎讓人覺得難以打破。

paragraphs.en: I'll bet you can relate. See if the following scenarios sound familiar.
paragraphs.zh: 我敢說你一定有同感。看看下面這些情境是不是很熟悉。

paragraphs.en: * You commit to eating healthy. After doing so successfully for a week, you stumble upon your favorite junk food. You're unable to resist, and there goes your diet.
paragraphs.zh: * 你決心要健康飲食。成功執行一週後,你不小心遇到了你最愛的垃圾食物。你抵擋不住誘惑,於是你的飲食計畫就這樣泡湯了。

paragraphs.en: * You commit to writing in a journal each morning. After a month, you inadvertently skip a day. You don't mean to do so. You just forget, and there goes your month-long streak.
paragraphs.zh: * 你決心每天早上寫日記。一個月後,你不小心漏掉了一天。你並非故意,只是忘記了,於是維持了一個月的連續紀錄就這樣中斷了。

paragraphs.en: * You tell yourself that you're going to visit the gym each afternoon after you get home from work. And you do so for a few weeks. Then, one day, you arrive home feeling exhausted. It was a particularly stressful day at your job, and you want nothing more than to relax with a glass of wine and Netflix. There goes your gym routine.
paragraphs.zh: * 你告訴自己下班回家後每天下午都要去健身房。你確實做到了好幾週。然後有一天,你拖著疲憊的身軀回到家。那天工作特別累人,你只想來杯紅酒配Netflix放鬆一下。於是你的健身routine就這樣被打斷了。

paragraphs.en: All of us go through this when we adopt new habits. We stumble. We make mistakes. It's a natural part of the process.
paragraphs.zh: 每個人在採納新習慣時都會經歷這些。我們會跌跌撞撞,會犯錯。這是整個過程中很自然的一部分。

paragraphs.en: It doesn't matter how important the habits are. They might completely transform our lives. Yet we still manage to slip up.
paragraphs.zh: 無論這些習慣有多重要——即使它們可能徹底改變我們的人生——我們仍然難免會失手。

paragraphs.en: Frustrating, right?
paragraphs.zh: 很令人沮喪,對吧?

paragraphs.en: When this happens, don't beat yourself up about it. Don't think of these misfires as failures. Think of them as minor hiccups.
paragraphs.zh: 當這種情況發生時,別苛責自己。別把這些失誤當作失敗,把它們當成小小的顛簸就好。

paragraphs.en: Here are three things you can do to quickly get back on track. They've worked for me, and I'll bet they'll work for you, too.
paragraphs.zh: 以下是三件能幫你快速重回正軌的事。它們對我很有效,我敢說對你也一樣管用。

paragraphs.en: #1 - Take a small step back
paragraphs.zh: #1 - 稍微退後一步

paragraphs.en: One of the keys to adopting any new habit is to take micro steps. Start small and build slowly.
paragraphs.zh: 養成任何新習慣的關鍵之一,就是採取「微小步驟」。從小處著手,慢慢累積。

paragraphs.en: For example, suppose you want to jog for 45 minutes each morning. Start by jogging for 5 minutes for a few days. Then, jog for 10 minutes over the next few days. Then, do it for 15 minutes the following week. And so on.
paragraphs.zh: 舉例來說,假設你想每天早上慢跑45分鐘。可以先從連續幾天慢跑5分鐘開始。接下來幾天慢跑10分鐘。再下一週做到15分鐘,依此類推。

paragraphs.en: Now, let's say you miss a few days. No problem. Take a step back. For example, if you've been jogging for 30 minutes a day and slip up, commit to jogging for just 20 minutes tomorrow. Or even 10 minutes.
paragraphs.zh: 現在,假設你漏了幾天。沒關係,退後一步就好。舉例來說,如果你原本每天慢跑30分鐘卻失手了,那就承諾明天只慢跑20分鐘,甚至10分鐘也行。

paragraphs.en: Making a smaller commitment will help get you back in the saddle.
paragraphs.zh: 訂下較小的承諾,能幫助你重新回到軌道上。

paragraphs.en: #2 - Put the habit on your daily schedule
paragraphs.zh: #2 - 把這個習慣排進你的每日行程

paragraphs.en: Make it an appointment with yourself.
paragraphs.zh: 把它當作與自己的一個約定。

paragraphs.en: For example, let's say you're committed to practicing the guitar each day. But your life gets busy, and you abandon the habit.
paragraphs.zh: 舉例來說,假設你決心每天練習吉他,但生活變得忙碌,於是你放棄了這個習慣。

paragraphs.en: Get back on track by putting your daily practice session on your schedule. Don't just put it on your to-do list. Actually block off time on your daily calendar.
paragraphs.zh: 把每日練習時段排進你的行事曆中,藉此重回正軌。不要只是把它列在待辦清單上,而是要在每日行事曆上真正劃出時間。

paragraphs.en: Treat it like an important, can't-miss appointment.
paragraphs.zh: 把它當作一個重要、不可錯過的約會來對待。

paragraphs.en: #3 - Commit to doing just a tiny bit
paragraphs.zh: #3 - 承諾只做一點點就好

paragraphs.en: It's funny how the brain works. We pride ourselves on being rational, reasonable, and logical, but we can actually trick our brains into doing something it doesn't want to do.
paragraphs.zh: 大腦的運作方式很有趣。我們自豪於自己是理性、講道理、有邏輯的,但實際上我們可以「欺騙」自己的大腦去做它原本不想做的事。

paragraphs.en: This can be very useful when we're trying to form new habits and need to get back on track after screwing up.
paragraphs.zh: 當我們想養成新習慣,並在搞砸後需要重回正軌時,這一招特別有用。

paragraphs.en: Tell yourself that you'll do just a tiny bit.
paragraphs.zh: 告訴自己,你只需要做一點點就好。

paragraphs.en: For example, suppose you're committed to working out for 45 minutes a day. You have an entire workout regimen. But for whatever reason, you skip a day. You just don't feel like working out. Then, you skip another day. And another.
paragraphs.zh: 舉例來說,假設你決心每天運動45分鐘,你有一整套完整的健身計畫。但不知為何,你跳過了一天,就是提不起勁運動。接著你又跳過了一天,再一天。

paragraphs.en: After skipping workouts for an entire week, getting back on track may seem impossible.
paragraphs.zh: 整整跳過一週的運動後,重回正軌似乎變得遙不可及。

paragraphs.en: Try this: tell yourself that you'll just do five pushups. Forget your carefully-planned regimen. Just focus on doing five pushups.
paragraphs.zh: 試試這個方法:告訴自己只要做五下伏地挺身就好。忘掉你精心規劃的整套計畫,只專注在完成五下伏地挺身。

paragraphs.en: Once you start, your mind will want to continue. That's what I mean by "tricking your brain." It's like persuading your child to try a new food you're certain he'll love. Focus on getting him to take the first bite.
paragraphs.zh: 一旦你開始了,你的心智就會想繼續下去。這就是我所謂的「欺騙大腦」。這就像哄你的孩子嘗試一種你確信他會喜歡的新食物——重點是先讓他咬下第一口。

paragraphs.en: Adopting new habits is rarely easy. Often we have to change years of mental programming before we can accept the new routines. Missteps are inevitable.
paragraphs.zh: 養成新習慣很少是件容易的事。我們通常必須改變多年來的心智慣性,才能接受新的routine。失誤在所難免。

paragraphs.en: The good news is, you can easily bounce back if you slip up. Try the three "tricks" above. You may be surprised by how effective they are.
paragraphs.zh: 好消息是,一旦失手,你也能輕鬆地重回正軌。試試上面這三個「小訣竅」,你可能會驚訝於它們有多有效。

paragraphs.en: I've bent your ear long enough today. My next email will be much shorter. I promise. :)
paragraphs.zh: 今天已經佔用你不少時間了。我保證下一封信會短很多。:)

paragraphs.en: Talk soon,
paragraphs.zh: 咱們再聊,

paragraphs.en: Damon
paragraphs.zh: Damon

paragraphs.en: P.S. If you're struggling to form new habits, my book Small Habits Revolution can help. It describes, in step-by-step detail, how to adopt new habits and make them stick.
paragraphs.zh: P.S. 如果你正為養成新習慣所苦,我的書《Small Habits Revolution》能幫上忙。書中以逐步詳盡的方式,說明如何採納新習慣並讓它們持續下去。

emails.subject: 5 personality traits that increase the odds you'll procrastinate

paragraphs.en: Hey 張振輝,
paragraphs.zh: 嗨 張振輝,

paragraphs.en: If you struggle with procrastination, you're not alone. Putting off until tomorrow that which we can do today is human nature.
paragraphs.zh: 如果你有拖延的問題,你並不孤單。把今天能做的事延到明天,是人類的天性。

paragraphs.en: In fact, evidence suggests that procrastination is linked to our personalities. Certain traits make us more likely to stall and postpone things.
paragraphs.zh: 事實上,有證據顯示拖延與我們的人格特質有關。某些特質會讓我們更容易拖延、延後事情。

paragraphs.en: Today, we'll cover five such traits. I can tell you from personal experience they definitely contribute to a tendency to procrastinate.
paragraphs.zh: 今天,我們就來談談五種這樣的特質。以我個人經驗來說,我可以告訴你,它們確實會助長拖延的傾向。

paragraphs.en: #1 - The Constant Worrier
paragraphs.zh: #1 - 「時刻擔憂型」

paragraphs.en: If you're always worried about catastrophes looming around the corner, it'll be difficult to take action. You'll be anxious that your actions might cause a catastrophe.
paragraphs.zh: 如果你總是擔心災難即將降臨,那麼採取行動就會變得困難。你會擔心自己的行動可能會招致災難。

paragraphs.en: Naturally, you'll be tempted to wait until circumstances seem safer and more certain.
paragraphs.zh: 自然而然地,你會傾向等到情況看起來更安全、更確定時再行動。

paragraphs.en: #2 - The Incessant Perfectionist
paragraphs.zh: #2 - 「無止盡的完美主義型」

paragraphs.en: If getting every detail right and making zero mistakes is a priority to you, you're going to put off tasks and projects.
paragraphs.zh: 如果把每個細節做到完美、零失誤視為優先要務,你就會不斷拖延任務與專案。

paragraphs.en: Sometimes, it'll be a matter of poor time management. You'll spend an inordinate amount of time perfecting something, ignoring everything else in the process. Other times, it's be due to anxiety and unrealistic expectations. You'll be unable to act because you'll be afraid that whatever you do won't be good enough.
paragraphs.zh: 有時候,這是時間管理不佳的問題——你會花費過多時間去完善某件事,而在這過程中忽略了其他一切。有時候,則是源於焦慮與不切實際的期待——你會因為害怕自己做的事不夠好,而遲遲無法行動。

paragraphs.en: I dealt this beast for many years. If you're a perfectionist, I know what you're going through.
paragraphs.zh: 我曾與這頭「猛獸」纏鬥多年。如果你是完美主義者,我完全懂你正在經歷什麼。

paragraphs.en: #3 - The Perpetual Idealist
paragraphs.zh: #3 - 「永恆的理想主義型」

paragraphs.en: It's okay to daydream. Indulging in fantasies about things we want to achieve is harmless...
paragraphs.zh: 做白日夢並無不可。沉浸在對想達成之事的幻想中是無害的……

paragraphs.en: ... as long as the daydreams are short-lived.
paragraphs.zh: ……只要這些白日夢是短暫的。

paragraphs.en: The problem comes when we dwell on the ideal and never manage to create a detailed action plan. Without a plan in place, we end up postponing things, telling ourselves "someday."
paragraphs.zh: 問題出在,當我們一直沉溺於理想,卻始終無法制定出具體的行動計畫時。沒有計畫,我們最終只會一再拖延,告訴自己「總有一天」。

paragraphs.en: #4 - The Self-Perceived Imposter
paragraphs.zh: #4 - 「自認冒牌者型」

paragraphs.en: Despite your past accomplishments, you may feel inadequate to tackle the task in front of you. Perhaps you feel you deserve neither the responsibility nor others' confidence.
paragraphs.zh: 儘管你過去有所成就,你可能仍覺得自己不足以應付眼前的任務。也許你覺得自己不配擁有這份責任,也不配得到他人的信任。

paragraphs.en: This is called "imposter syndrome." You chalk up your past successes as owing to luck rather than your skills. And because you can't rely on luck, you have trouble getting started.
paragraphs.zh: 這叫做「冒牌者症候群」。你把過去的成功歸功於運氣,而非自己的能力。而由於你無法「依賴」運氣,你就很難開始行動。

paragraphs.en: #5 - The Overwhelmed
paragraphs.zh: #5 - 「不堪重負型」

paragraphs.en: When you're drowning under a flood of responsibilities, expectations, and emotions, it seems impossible to take action. It feels like there's too much on your plate.
paragraphs.zh: 當你被排山倒海的責任、期待與情緒淹沒時,採取行動似乎變得不可能。你會感覺自己肩上的擔子太多太重。

paragraphs.en: Making matters worse, your inner critic gets into the act, telling you that you're feeling overwhelmed because you're not good enough to handle everything.
paragraphs.zh: 更糟的是,你內心的批評者這時也跳出來插一腳,告訴你之所以感到不堪重負,是因為你不夠好,無法應付這一切。

paragraphs.en: So you procrastinate.
paragraphs.zh: 於是你就拖延了。

paragraphs.en: I won't bore you with my personal horror stories about this stuff. Suffice to say, if you deal with any of the above, I relate and empathize.
paragraphs.zh: 我就不用自己的親身慘痛經歷來煩你了。總之,如果你也面臨上述任何一種情況,我完全能感同身受。

paragraphs.en: The good news is, you can train yourself to take action when you feel like stalling. It doesn't require purging the above personality traits. Rather, it's a matter of being aware of them and refusing to let them control you.
paragraphs.zh: 好消息是,即使你想拖延,你也能訓練自己採取行動。這並不需要根除上述的人格特質,而是需要覺察它們,並拒絕讓它們主宰你。

paragraphs.en: I have some ideas to share on the matter, but this email is already long enough.
paragraphs.zh: 關於這個主題我還有些想法想分享,但這封信已經夠長了。

paragraphs.en: We'll revisit this in the near future.
paragraphs.zh: 我們近期會再回頭談這個話題。

paragraphs.en: Talk soon,
paragraphs.zh: 咱們再聊,

paragraphs.en: Damon
paragraphs.zh: Damon

paragraphs.en: P.S. If you're tired of procrastinating and want to break the habit, you may find my book The Procrastination Cure helpful. It's filled with the tactics I used to train myself to stop putting things off. I'll bet many of them will work for you, too.
paragraphs.zh: P.S. 如果你厭倦了拖延,想要戒掉這個習慣,你可能會覺得我的書《The Procrastination Cure》很有幫助。書中充滿了我用來訓練自己停止拖延的各種戰術。我敢說其中許多也會對你有效。

emails.subject: Here's how to prioritize when you're overwhelmed by your to-do list

paragraphs.en: Hey 張振輝,
paragraphs.zh: 嗨 張振輝,

paragraphs.en: Ever had one of those days when your to-do list is a mile long and there's just not enough time to do everything?
paragraphs.zh: 你是否有過這樣的日子:待辦清單長得沒完沒了,時間卻怎麼也不夠用?

paragraphs.en: Making matters worse, people keep demanding your attention and asking for your help.
paragraphs.zh: 更糟的是,還有人不斷要求你的注意力,請你幫忙。

paragraphs.en: Yeah, we've all had those days. Frustrating, right?
paragraphs.zh: 是啊,我們都經歷過這種日子。很令人沮喪,對吧?

paragraphs.en: That's when it becomes critical to prioritize tasks. If we don't, we risk getting buried under a mountain of to-do items, some of which aren't even important to us.
paragraphs.zh: 這時候,「排定任務優先順序」就變得至關重要。如果不這麼做,我們就有可能被堆積如山的待辦事項淹沒,而其中有些甚至根本不重要。

paragraphs.en: Today, I'm going to share a method for separating the stuff you must get done from the stuff that only seems consequential.
paragraphs.zh: 今天,我要跟你分享一個方法,用來區分「必須完成的事」與「只是看起來很重要的事」。

paragraphs.en: It's not my method. It springs from something former U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower said back in the 50s.
paragraphs.zh: 這不是我發明的方法。它源自美國前總統艾森豪(Dwight D. Eisenhower)在1950年代說過的一句話。

paragraphs.en: He said, "I have two kinds of problems: the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent."
paragraphs.zh: 他說:「我有兩種問題:緊急的與重要的。緊急的事通常不重要,重要的事則從來不緊急。」

paragraphs.en: That became known as the Eisenhower Principle. And it's a terrific way to manage your workload, whether you're at home or in the office.
paragraphs.zh: 這後來被稱為「艾森豪原則」。無論是在家裡還是在辦公室,這都是管理工作量的絕佳方法。

paragraphs.en: Here's how it works...
paragraphs.zh: 運作方式是這樣的……

paragraphs.en: URGENT describes things that need your attention right now.
paragraphs.zh: 「緊急」指的是需要你立刻處理的事。

paragraphs.en: IMPORTANT describes things that'll help you to achieve a desired outcome.
paragraphs.zh: 「重要」指的是有助於你達成期望結果的事。

paragraphs.en: With that in mind, create the following four lists:
paragraphs.zh: 有了這個概念後,建立以下四個清單:

paragraphs.en: 1. Important and urgent
paragraphs.zh: 1. 重要且緊急

paragraphs.en: 2. Important but not urgent
paragraphs.zh: 2. 重要但不緊急

paragraphs.en: 3. Not important but urgent
paragraphs.zh: 3. 不重要但緊急

paragraphs.en: 4. Not important and not urgent
paragraphs.zh: 4. 不重要也不緊急

paragraphs.en: Next, assign every to-do item to one of these four lists.
paragraphs.zh: 接著,把每一項待辦事項分配到這四個清單中的其中一個。

paragraphs.en: List #1 is reserved for tasks that not only demand your immediate attention, but will also help you to reach your goals. If you're a student, this might mean finishing an assignment on deadline. If you work from home, it could include finishing a project for a client.
paragraphs.zh: 清單一保留給那些不僅需要你立即處理、也有助於你達成目標的任務。如果你是學生,這可能表示要準時完成一份作業;如果你在家工作,則可能包括為客戶完成一項專案。

paragraphs.en: List #2 is where you'll put tasks that'll help you to achieve your goals, but don't require your attention at this moment. Examples include exercising, meditating, or planning a date night for you and your spouse.
paragraphs.zh: 清單二則放那些有助於達成目標、但當下不需要你立刻處理的任務。例如運動、冥想,或為你和伴侶規劃一個約會之夜。

paragraphs.en: List #3 is for tasks that demand your immediate attention, but contribute nothing toward your goals. At the office, this might include random phone calls or coworkers who stop by to chat. At home, this could include a friend or family member who stops by unannounced.
paragraphs.zh: 清單三放那些需要你立即處理、但對你的目標毫無幫助的任務。在辦公室,這可能包括突如其來的電話,或是同事跑來閒聊;在家中,這可能包括未事先告知就來訪的朋友或家人。

paragraphs.en: List #4 is for distractions. It's for the stuff you WANT to do that won't contribute to any desired outcome. Stuff that's neither urgent nor important. This is where you'll put things like binge-watching Grey's Anatomy or The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, playing Fortnight or Minecraft, or catching up on Instagram.
paragraphs.zh: 清單四是給干擾事項用的。這是那些你「想」做、但對任何期望結果都沒有貢獻的事——既不緊急也不重要的事。像是一口氣追完《實習醫生》或《漫才梅索太太》、玩《Fortnite》或《Minecraft》,或是滑Instagram。

paragraphs.en: You've done the hard part. Now, it's just a matter of focusing your attention.
paragraphs.zh: 困難的部分你已經做完了。現在,只剩下把注意力集中起來而已。

paragraphs.en: Spend the majority of your time and energy completing tasks found on List #1 and List #2. That's where you'll have the greatest impact. If you have time left over, address the stuff on the other two lists.
paragraphs.zh: 把大部分的時間與精力,花在完成清單一與清單二上的任務。那裡才是你能發揮最大影響力的地方。如果還有剩餘時間,再處理另外兩個清單上的事。

paragraphs.en: And if you don't have time (or energy) for them, don't be afraid to let them go. After all, they're not going to help you to reach your goals.
paragraphs.zh: 如果你沒有時間(或精力)處理它們,也不用害怕放手。畢竟,它們並不會幫助你達成目標。

paragraphs.en: Let's Sum It Up
paragraphs.zh: 總結一下

paragraphs.en: Some tasks are important. Some are urgent. Some are both. And some are neither.
paragraphs.zh: 有些任務重要,有些緊急,有些兩者兼具,有些兩者皆非。

paragraphs.en: Allocating your time accordingly will prevent you from getting overwhelmed when you have more demands on your time than time itself.
paragraphs.zh: 依此分配你的時間,能讓你在時間需求超過時間本身時,不至於被壓垮。

paragraphs.en: Talk soon,
paragraphs.zh: 咱們再聊,

paragraphs.en: Damon
paragraphs.zh: Damon

paragraphs.en: P.S. A lot of folks create to-do lists without a clear strategy. Important tasks fall through the cracks, which gets intensely frustrating over time. If you're struggling with this common issue, I encourage you to check out my book To-Do List Formula.
paragraphs.zh: P.S. 很多人在建立待辦清單時,都沒有清楚的策略。重要任務因此被漏掉,久而久之會讓人非常沮喪。如果你也為這個常見問題所苦,我鼓勵你看看我的書《To-Do List Formula》。

emails.subject: 3 simple (and unorthodox) hacks to improve your focus

paragraphs.en: Hey 張振輝,
paragraphs.zh: 嗨 張振輝,

paragraphs.en: The last few emails I've sent you have been pretty long. So, let's keep this one short.
paragraphs.zh: 我最近寄給你的幾封信都相當長。所以,這封信我們就長話短說。

paragraphs.en: Today, I'm going to share with you 3 unconventional tips that'll improve your focus and help you to fight distractions. By "unconventional" I mean they're outside the normal fare.
paragraphs.zh: 今天,我要跟你分享3個能提升專注力、幫助你對抗分心的另類技巧。所謂「另類」,是指它們不是一般常見的做法。

paragraphs.en: Each one is simple and easy to practice. That means you can use them starting today.
paragraphs.zh: 每一個都很簡單、容易上手,這表示你今天就可以開始使用。

paragraphs.en: Enough blather. Let's jump right in.
paragraphs.zh: 廢話不多說,我們直接進入正題。

paragraphs.en: Unconventional Tip #1 - Work on Something Entirely Different
paragraphs.zh: 另類技巧 #1 - 做一件完全不同的事

paragraphs.en: When you can't concentrate, give yourself something to do that's a total departure from whatever you're working on.
paragraphs.zh: 當你無法專注時,給自己找件事做,一件與你正在進行的工作完全無關的事。

paragraphs.en: For example, let's say you're working on a boring spreadsheet, and your mind keeps wandering. Get some paper and start journaling for a few minutes. Or create song lyrics. Or come up with a witty haiku.
paragraphs.zh: 舉例來說,假設你正在處理一份無聊的試算表,思緒卻不斷飄走。這時拿張紙,寫幾分鐘日記;或創作幾句歌詞;或想一首俏皮的俳句。

paragraphs.en: Or let's say you're writing a novel, and you keep getting distracted. Grab some paper and do a few math problems. For example, multiply 32,537 and 64,319.
paragraphs.zh: 又或者,假設你正在寫小說,卻不斷分心。這時拿張紙,做幾道數學題,例如計算32,537乘以64,319。

paragraphs.en: Sound silly? Don't dismiss it. You may find that it stimulates your brain in a way that lets you get back to the task at hand with renewed focus.
paragraphs.zh: 聽起來很傻氣?別急著否定它。你可能會發現,這樣的做法能以某種方式刺激大腦,讓你能以煥然一新的專注力回到手邊的任務。

paragraphs.en: Unconventional Tip #2 - Take a Break
paragraphs.zh: 另類技巧 #2 - 休息一下

paragraphs.en: When we get distracted, it's tempting to fight through the distraction. We tell ourselves, "C'mon. Get it together. Stop being such a ninny. FOCUS!"
paragraphs.zh: 當我們分心時,很容易想硬撐著抵抗分心。我們告訴自己:「拜託,振作點,別再這麼沒用了,專心點!」

paragraphs.en: We get frustrated with ourselves, which, ironically, makes us more distracted. That, in turn, amps up our frustration.
paragraphs.zh: 我們對自己感到挫折,而諷刺的是,這反而讓我們更加分心。這又進一步加深了我們的挫折感。

paragraphs.en: It's a terrible cycle.
paragraphs.zh: 這是個很糟糕的惡性循環。

paragraphs.en: What we should do is take a break.
paragraphs.zh: 我們真正該做的,是休息一下。

paragraphs.en: When you're unable to concentrate, stop what you're doing. Stand up (if you're sitting). Walk away. Get a glass of water. Take a 10-minute walk outside. Get some fresh air.
paragraphs.zh: 當你無法集中注意力時,停下手邊的事。站起來(如果你正坐著)、走開一下、喝杯水、到外面散步10分鐘、呼吸點新鮮空氣。

paragraphs.en: You'll be surprised at how well it clears the mind.
paragraphs.zh: 你會驚訝於這樣做能多有效地清空思緒。

paragraphs.en: Unconventional Tip #3 - Clear Your Workspace
paragraphs.zh: 另類技巧 #3 - 清理你的工作空間

paragraphs.en: My office used to be a pigsty. Dirt and grime weren't the problems. Paper was. Snail mail, stuff I printed from my computer, countless files, etc.
paragraphs.zh: 我的辦公室以前簡直是個豬窩。問題不在於灰塵或髒污,而在於「紙張」——郵寄信件、從電腦印出來的東西、數不清的檔案等等。

paragraphs.en: The clutter destroyed my ability to focus. Everything distracted me.
paragraphs.zh: 這些雜亂徹底摧毀了我的專注力。所有東西都讓我分心。

paragraphs.en: Can you guess what happened when I cleared my workspace? Suddenly, I could manage the distractions. I was finally able to concentrate.
paragraphs.zh: 你猜當我清理好工作空間後發生了什麼事?突然間,我能夠應付那些干擾了。我終於能夠專心了。

paragraphs.en: I have a lot more unorthodox hacks for improving your focus. But let's stop here for today. I wanted to keep this email short and it's already getting a bit too long.
paragraphs.zh: 我還有更多提升專注力的非傳統技巧,但今天就先講到這裡。我原本想讓這封信保持簡短,結果已經有點太長了。

paragraphs.en: Try the above tips. And let me know if they help!
paragraphs.zh: 試試上面這些技巧,並讓我知道它們有沒有幫助!

paragraphs.en: Talk soon,
paragraphs.zh: 咱們再聊,

paragraphs.en: Damon
paragraphs.zh: Damon

paragraphs.en: P.S. If you're having trouble concentrating, you're not alone. Everyone deals with this problem. You may find my book Fast Focus to be the solution you need. In it, I describe the tactics that worked for me.
paragraphs.zh: P.S. 如果你在專注力上遇到困難,你並不孤單,每個人都會面臨這個問題。你可能會發現我的書《Fast Focus》正是你需要的解方。書中描述了對我有效的各種戰術。

emails.subject: How to take criticism like a pro (without feeling like a failure)

paragraphs.en: Hey 張振輝,
paragraphs.zh: 嗨 張振輝,

paragraphs.en: I used to hate criticism.
paragraphs.zh: 我以前很討厭被批評。

paragraphs.en: Whenever someone pointed out something I had done wrong, I'd get defensive. I'd argue. I'd become suspicious of their motivations.
paragraphs.zh: 每當有人指出我做錯的地方,我就會變得防衛心很重。我會爭辯,會開始懷疑對方的動機。

paragraphs.en: And I'm ashamed to admit, I'd find something I found lacking in THEM and go on the offensive. I'd attack.
paragraphs.zh: 而且我很慚愧地承認,我還會反過來挑出對方的缺點,展開反擊。我會攻擊對方。

paragraphs.en: To say I lacked grace when confronted with criticism is the understatement of a lifetime.
paragraphs.zh: 說我在面對批評時缺乏氣度,實在是這輩子最輕描淡寫的說法了。

paragraphs.en: I wanted everyone to think everything I did was perfect. So disapproval was a personal attack on me.
paragraphs.zh: 我希望每個人都認為我做的每件事都完美無缺,所以任何不認同對我而言都是人身攻擊。

paragraphs.en: At least, that was my perspective back then. I'm not proud of it.
paragraphs.zh: 至少,那是我當時的想法。我對此並不引以為傲。

paragraphs.en: I've since let go of my inner perfectionist. I've learned to not only accept constructive criticism, but look forward to it.
paragraphs.zh: 後來,我逐漸放下了心中的完美主義。我學會不僅接受建設性的批評,甚至還開始期待它。

paragraphs.en: And it has made a HUGE difference in my life. It has improved the way I communicate. It has helped me to refine how I write books. It has allowed me to handle problems with less frustration and more insight.
paragraphs.zh: 這為我的人生帶來了「巨大」的改變。它改善了我溝通的方式,幫助我精進寫書的方式,也讓我能以更少的挫折感、更多的洞察力去處理問題。

paragraphs.en: Let's say you're in the same boat I was. Let's suppose you loathe constructive criticism. You know deep inside that you should be open to it. But it's hard to get there.
paragraphs.zh: 假設你和我當年一樣,厭惡建設性批評。你內心深處知道自己應該對此保持開放,但很難真正做到。

paragraphs.en: Here are a few tips that worked for me...
paragraphs.zh: 以下是幾個對我有效的訣竅……

paragraphs.en: 1. Don't react.
paragraphs.zh: 1. 別立刻反應。

paragraphs.en: I know, it's instinctive. But try to suppress the instinct. Try not to furrow your brow or scrunch up your face. And don't be like me in years past, responding "Yeah? Well, you're terrible, also!"
paragraphs.zh: 我知道,這是本能反應。但試著壓下這個本能。試著別皺眉、別擺臭臉。也別像我當年那樣,回嘴說:「是喔?那你也很爛啊!」

paragraphs.en: 2. Ask yourself, "Will this feedback help me?"
paragraphs.zh: 2. 問問自己:「這個回饋對我有幫助嗎?」

paragraphs.en: Chances are, the criticism highlights something you can improve. If so, you can benefit by taking it to heart. Why not take advantage of it?
paragraphs.zh: 很有可能,這個批評指出了你可以改進的地方。如果是這樣,把它放在心上對你會有益處。為什麼不好好利用它呢?

paragraphs.en: 3. Recognize that the person giving feedback isn't trying to tear you down.
paragraphs.zh: 3. 認清給你回饋的人並非想要打擊你。

paragraphs.en: People who are kind enough to offer constructive feedback truly want to help you.
paragraphs.zh: 願意善意提供建設性回饋的人,是真心想幫助你的。

paragraphs.en: Oh sure, we've all dealt with people who "offer feedback" as a weapon. But in my experience, they're in the minority. And hopefully you're avoiding such people because they're a bummer to hang around.
paragraphs.zh: 當然,我們都遇過把「提供回饋」當作武器的人。但依我的經驗,這樣的人是少數。希望你也懂得避開這類讓人相處起來很掃興的人。

paragraphs.en: MOST folks are eager to help.
paragraphs.zh: 「大多數」人其實都是樂於幫忙的。

paragraphs.en: 4. Ask questions to clarify the feedback.
paragraphs.zh: 4. 提出問題,釐清回饋的內容。

paragraphs.en: Constructive criticism usually starts out bland. The person giving it doesn't want to offend you. To get to the juicy details, the stuff that's really helpful, you need to ask questions.
paragraphs.zh: 建設性批評通常一開始都說得很含糊。提出批評的人不想冒犯你。要挖出真正有價值、有幫助的細節,你需要主動發問。

paragraphs.en: For example, suppose a friend says, "I've noticed you're often distracted when we talk." You might ask, "Can you tell me the last time you noticed that?"
paragraphs.zh: 舉例來說,假設一位朋友說:「我注意到我們聊天時你常常分心。」你可以問:「你可以告訴我,你最近一次注意到是什麼時候嗎?」

paragraphs.en: The circumstances surrounding your distraction might reveal why it's happening and how you can stop it.
paragraphs.zh: 那些造成你分心的具體情境,或許能揭露出原因,以及你該如何停止這種情況。

paragraphs.en: That's it for now.
paragraphs.zh: 今天就講到這裡。

paragraphs.en: Let's talk soon,
paragraphs.zh: 咱們再聊,

paragraphs.en: Damon
paragraphs.zh: Damon

paragraphs.en: P.S. If you struggle with perfectionism, I can definitely relate. You may find my book The Joy of Imperfection helpful, especially when it comes to taking constructive criticism.
paragraphs.zh: P.S. 如果你也為完美主義所苦,我完全能感同身受。你可能會覺得我的書《The Joy of Imperfection》很有幫助,尤其是在接受建設性批評這方面。
